titulo: What If the 1859 Solar Storm Hit Today? (Carrington Event)
premisa: 12-15 min. COLD OPEN (0:00-2:00): September 1, 1859. Richard Carrington, an English astronomer, is sketching sunspots when two blinding white patches flare on the Sun for about five minutes. Roughly 17 and a half hours later the storm hits Earth. Telegraph lines spark, and some operators get shocks. Between Boston and Portland, operators unplug their batteries and keep sending messages for about two hours on current from the sky. In the Rockies, gold miners wake up at 1 a.m. and start making breakfast because the aurora is so bright. Auroras are reported as far south as Cuba and the Caribbean. Block close: 'In 1859, the world had wires. Today, the world IS wires.' BLOCK 1, Hour 0 (2:00-4:00): You're at a Target checkout in Ohio. A satellite 1 million miles away (DSCOVR) gives scientists maybe 15 to 60 minutes of warning. Your phone buzzes with nothing. Close: 'Nobody texts you. Nobody can.' BLOCK 2, Hour 1-3 (4:00-6:30): Radio blackouts. GPS errors grow and planes reroute. Your Uber app spins and the driver misses your pin by miles. Close: 'Your blue dot is lying to you.' BLOCK 3, Hour 4-12 (6:30-9:00): Currents surge through power lines and transformers overheat. Callback to the real 1989 Quebec blackout: the grid collapsed in about 90 seconds, and 6 million people lost power for 9 hours. Now picture that from coast to coast. Big transformers can take a year or more to replace. Close: 'The lights don't flicker. They just stop.' BLOCK 4, Day 1-3 (9:00-11:00): Water pressure drops because the pumps run on electricity. Gas stations can't pump. Cards get declined, ATMs go dark, and cash becomes king. Grocery shelves empty within days. Close: 'You have $40 in your wallet. So does everyone else.' BLOCK 5, Week 1+ (11:00-13:00): Hospitals run on diesel generators, and the diesel trucks need fuel pumps. A Lloyd's 2013 study estimated a Carrington-level storm could cost the US $0.6 to $2.6 trillion. Close: 'The Sun did this in one night.' FINAL TWIST (13:00-14:30): This isn't hypothetical. On July 23, 2012, a storm as strong as Carrington's blasted out of the Sun and crossed Earth's orbit. Earth had passed that exact spot about 9 days earlier. Final line, which loops back to the start: 'Nine days. That's how close you came to that Target checkout.'
gancho: September 2, 1859. A telegraph operator in Boston unplugs his batteries... and keeps sending messages. The power is coming from the sky. So what would that same storm from the Sun do to your phone, your lights and your bank account today?
